name: hyperframes
description: Read first to make, edit, animate or render any video with HyperFrames (HTML rendered to video), including launch films, explainers, music videos, charts, maps, vertical clips, title cards, captions and overlays. # HyperFrames

HyperFrames renders HTML to video by seeking a paused timeline frame by frame, so every render is identical; the person edits the same files in the Studio preview. Use it unless another framework or a plain browser recording is asked for. Run the CLI as `npx hyperframes <command>` (`/hyperframes-cli`); at the start of a new video, `npx hyperframes usage --json` reports the person's remaining plan usage (say "unknown" when it is).

`index.html` is the root composition: it declares the video's variables and mounts one scene per sub-composition from `compositions/`. Media and fonts live in `assets/`. A new project: `npx hyperframes init <dir>`. A website as the subject: `npx hyperframes capture <url> --json`.

Build what was asked: no voiceover or captions and no new aspect ratio unless the request or the source calls for them; a film over ~15 s that tells something gets music and sound on its visible actions unless the person asked for silence (`references/sound.md`). A new video is 1920×1080 at 30 fps. A question, a hold or a loose idea gets an answer or a proposal, not an edit. Before hand-writing a named effect, transition, caption style, chart or card, search the registry (`/hyperframes-registry`). Any media (a presenter or avatar, footage, voice, music): `/media-use`, which says when HeyGen is needed and what is free. Show real things from their source (the product's screens, the brand's logo, a real place's imagery); draw only what has none.

## Contract

`npx hyperframes check --json` reports most violations with a `Fix:` line.

1. Every timed element has `class="clip"`, `data-start` and `data-duration` in seconds, and shows over `[start, start + duration)`: land an end state just before its end. `data-track-index` is only a Studio lane; paint order is `z-index`.
2. The video's length is the root's `data-duration`: overrun is cut, an early end holds the last frame.
3. Each composition builds one paused timeline and registers it after its tweens: `window.__timelines["<data-composition-id>"] = tl`.
4. No `Date.now()`, unseeded `Math.random()`, network fetches, timers or `repeat: -1`. Everything visible is a function of timeline time.
5. Never tween `display`, `visibility` or `autoAlpha` on a `.clip`; animate a child.
6. No CSS `transform` on an element GSAP transforms; animate transforms, not `left`/`top`/`width`/`height`.
7. Never `play()`, `pause()` or seek media. A `<video>` keeps its sound with `data-has-audio="true"`, else it is `muted`; music, voice, replacement sound and J/L cuts are a separate `<audio>`.
8. Every `<audio>` has an `id` or it is left out of the mix. No `crossorigin` on media. Time a `<video>` or its wrapper, never both.
9. Only the bundled fonts (`references/format.md`) resolve by name; any other family needs `@font-face` to a file in `assets/fonts/`.
10. Asset paths are root-relative (`assets/...`), in sub-compositions too.
11. Grades, grain, blur and vignettes on footage go through `npx hyperframes media-treatment` (`/media-use`), never CSS filters.
12. A scene file puts its styles, markup and scripts inside `<template>` and styles its root as `#root`. Intended overflow or overlap: `data-layout-allow-overflow`, `data-layout-allow-overlap`.

Studio edits the tags you write.

- One scene per sub-composition, short readable ids; the root holds only scene hosts, media and audio.
- Timed elements are written in the HTML, not made by script, each with a stable `id`.
- Copy, brand colours and swappable media are variables (`data-var-text`, `data-var-src`, `var(--id)`).
- One kind per track: `data-track-kind="graphics"` on scene and overlay hosts, `captions` on the one host that holds every caption group.
- Content stays inside the 90% action-safe box, captions and key text inside 80% title-safe; Studio draws the guides, never add them.

# Explainers, tutorials and "how it works"

One idea the viewer understands by the end (`../story.md` §1). The spine is one concrete example worked through, start to finish, not a tour of facts. Usually 30–90 s.

## Ground it first

Start where the viewer already is: a person, a place or a situation they know, and a question they would ask about it ("why does the astronaut come home younger than her twin?"). The abstract device (a light clock, a graph, a field) enters inside that situation, as the thing that answers the question, and the film returns to the person at the end with the answer. A film that opens on the device alone is a diagram, not an explainer.

## Devices that explain

- **The object is the explanation.** Build a thing whose working is the idea: a machine, a model, a map, a light clock, drawn so it reads as what it is (its material, its mount, where it sits in the scene). Every number on screen comes from it, and the camera tours through it: cutaways, an exploded view, a dive into the part that matters.
- **One diagram that grows.** Start from the simplest true picture and add one part per beat, each appearing when it is named; never a finished diagram dropped on screen at once.
- **Continuous transformation.** Each step morphs out of the last (a bar becomes an axis, a dot becomes a population), so the viewer never loses the thread to a cut.
- **The worked example.** One real input (a sentence, a number, a photo) travels through every step to the answer.

## Shapes of information

Most explainable lines are one of a few shapes, and each has its own picture: a number that lands (`data.md`); a myth turned over (the wrong idea struck through, the right one printed over it); before and after; many things converging into a few groups; a network that densifies; one chosen out of many; steps in order; a real screenshot with the detail circled; a quote set as a poster; a chapter card. Pick the shape first, then the picture, so similar lines get different pictures and every line gets the one that shows it.

## Words

- Narrated: the voice is the clock (`../sound.md` §2). Reveal each part when the voice names it, across the back half of the scene; keep a scene to about 19 spoken words (`../film.md` "Script and pacing").
- Not narrated: large lines carry it, up to about 10 words, each held 0.5 s + 0.3 s a word.
- Labels sit on the part they name, with a leader line when needed, and appear with it. No legends, no bullet slides.

## Getting it right

- Every claim, value and step traces to the source; a number the source did not give is left out or marked illustrative. One data module drives every figure so the numbers agree with each other.
- Check the science or the logic of each step before animating it; a beautiful wrong diagram is worse than none.
- End on the one idea in one line. No brand end card unless asked.

## Tells for this type

A slide of bullets; icons in circles; three cards in a row; the whole diagram at once; a narrator repeating the text on screen word for word.
# Story

Read before building any video that tells something over about 15 s: a launch or promo, an explainer, a pull-request or changelog video, a recap, a music video with a narrative. Most weak films are good motion around no story: a list of features, three cards in a row, a logo, a URL.

Skip it for an edit to an existing project, captions or overlays on footage, and a short single-idea piece (one kinetic line, a map move, a highlight on an image), where the request is the story. When the person gave a script, a storyboard or a reference film, follow theirs. The shape of each kind of film (launch, explainer, music, data, vertical, 3D, character) is in `types/`.

## 1. The one thing

- **What it is**, in one line: "You can now …" for a launch, the one idea the viewer must understand for an explainer, what changed and why it matters for a pull request. A whole release ("2.0", "what's new") is not one thing: take its headline.
- **The one thing to remember** after the film ends, in the viewer's words, not the brand slogan.
- **One viewer doing one real task**, from the moment they need it to the result. That task is the spine, and one real piece of data (a query, a file, a prompt, a number) travels through it from the hook to the payoff. An explainer's spine is one concrete example worked through.
- Keep facts (what it does, real numbers, real labels) apart from creative choices (angle, tone, look). Every claim on screen traces to the source: the site, the PR, the docs or the person's words. Use the person's own copy verbatim.
- What the source does not say stays unsaid: never derive a claim it did not make ("40 min to 2 min" is not "20× faster"), mark an example number as illustrative, and show a screen you cannot get as a labelled placeholder, not a drawn one.

## 2. Three storylines, then one

Write three. They are three different films, not three titles on one film: each has its own **world** (where it happens and what it looks like), its own **device** (what the story is) and its own **form** (how the camera and the cuts carry it). Sketch five or more ideas first, a line each pairing a device with a form (tables below); drop those the subject cannot carry well, and of the rest keep the three that differ most. Make one of the three the bold one you would not have picked first. Each says:

- its name, its device and form in a few words, and in two sentences what the viewer sees and feels;
- the first two seconds, exactly;
- its beats in one line (`hook → … → end card`);
- its look in one line: ground, type, the one material or treatment, taken from the subject or the brand (`look.md`);
- its sound in one line (`sound.md` §1).

The storylines are words: build nothing for any of them before one is picked. Pick a storyline for its story: the one a stranger would follow and remember, with people or a situation they know, ahead of the most striking picture. Picking a storyline picks its look and its sound.

# HyperFrames CLI

Run `npx hyperframes <command>` unless the project gives a wrapper; then use the wrapper. It needs Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg. Every command has `--help`; most take `--json`, and a failure prints `✗ …`, a `Fix:` line and exits non-zero.

## Commands by job

| Job | Commands |
| --- | --- |
| Start | `init <dir>` (blank; `--example <name>` only when asked), `capture <url>` |
| Read a project | `info`, `compositions`, `timeline --json`, `docs <topic>` |
| Check it | `lint` while writing; `check --json` as the gate (lint, runtime, layout, contrast) |
| Look at it | `snapshot` (`--at <t,…>`, `--range START,END`, `--composition <id>`, `--zoom`, `--angle`, `--against <video>`), `keyframes`, `compare`, `audio` |
| Edit the timeline | `timeline` with `move`, `trim`, `split`, `set`, `duplicate`, `delete`, `apply`, `undo`, `ids` |
| Reuse | `catalog`, `add` (`/hyperframes-registry`) |
| Media and sound | `media-treatment`, `grade-compare`, `remove-background`, `tts`, `transcribe`, `beats`, `normalize-audio` (`/media-use`) |
| Show and ship | `preview`, `present` (`/slideshow`), `render`, `publish`, `cloud`, `lambda`, `cloudrun` |
| Desktop app | `open`, `catch-up` |
| Upkeep | `doctor`, `browser`, `upgrade`, `skills`, `usage`, `clean`, `feedback` |

`validate`, `inspect` and `layout` are deprecated aliases of `check`; `events` is telemetry for skills' own scripts. Don't run them.

## The loop

1. Write, then `npx hyperframes lint` after the first pass and after structural changes.
2. `npx hyperframes check --json` and fix every error. While a lint error remains the layout and contrast audits don't run; "0 samples" means nothing was checked. Contrast failures carry a `suggestedColor`. A finding at a single sample (an entrance in flight) is info; a 3 s+ video with no visible change fails `sweep_static`.
3. `npx hyperframes snapshot` and read the PNGs (under `.hyperframes/artifacts/snapshots/`): that is how you see the video. With sub-compositions, snapshot a midpoint of every scene; tiny unstyled content or a missing hero is a mount defect (`../hyperframes/references/format.md`).

5. When it is time to render (step 4): `npx hyperframes render --quality looks --output out.mp4` (`draft` while iterating, `delivery` for the final). Confirm the file is non-empty and its `ffprobe` duration matches the root `data-duration`, then look at decoded frames.

"This element" or the current selection: `npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection`; `no-selection` means ask them to click it.

These are the edits Studio itself makes, so the result stays in Studio's shape.

- `timeline --json` lists clips with absolute `absStart`/`absEnd`, owning `file` and the `#id` ref the edit commands take (`timeline ids` stamps missing ids).
- `timeline move|trim|split|set|duplicate|delete <ref> … --plan --json` previews one edit; run it again without `--plan`. `--start`, `--end`, `--duration` set one edge or the length.
- An edit is refused when the clip would overlap a neighbour (`--overwrite`, or move the neighbour first) or end past its composition: raise the root's `data-duration` first. No command changes `data-duration`.
- Several edits at once: a JSON file such as `[{"verb": "move", "ref": "#outro", "time": "9"}]`, then `timeline apply plan.json --json`. Each run prints a `receipt`; save it and `timeline undo receipt.json` reverts it.

Every write is kept and can be undone. At the start of a turn, `npx hyperframes history begin --who <you> --label "<plan>"`, then `history --since mine --who <you>` to see what the person changed; build on their edits. A check failed or they say it got worse: `history undo --who <you>`, never hand-edit back. End the turn with `history end`.

| Need | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Local | `render --quality looks --output out.mp4` (`draft`, `delivery`) |
| Reproducible container | `render --docker --strict --output out.mp4` |
| Batch from variables | `render --batch rows.json --output "renders/{name}.mp4"` |
| Hosted, no local Chrome or FFmpeg | `cloud render` (`references/cloud.md`) |
| Your own AWS or GCP | `lambda render`, `cloudrun render` (`references/lambda.md`, `references/cloudrun.md`) |

# Review

You wrote the timeline, so you know what happens; the viewer sees it once, at full speed, often on a phone. Review is how you see the film as they will: as a harsh motion director, not a proud author. `check` catches what is broken; this pass catches what is weak. Run it after `check` passes, on every new film and on any edit that changes timing or layout, before you reply or render.

## 1. Measure, then look

1. `npx hyperframes check --json`. Besides errors it warns on craft it can measure: a line on screen too briefly to read (`line_unread`), more than 3 s with nothing changing (`dead_stretch`), text under 2.6% of the frame's short side (`text_below_floor`), an empty first frame (`first_frame_empty`, the thumbnail on social players), a film over 15 s with no sound (`film_silent`). A warning is a question, not a rule: fix it, or keep it on purpose and say why in the note (a deliberate hold carries `data-hold`).
2. `npx hyperframes snapshot --review` writes three sheets: each scene just after it starts and at its middle, plus each `data-beat`, a strip across every cut (−0.2 s to +0.2 s), and the beat frames at phone width (360 px). Open all three.
3. Motion between the beats: `snapshot --range START,END --frames 8` around the hero move and the payoff; `keyframes --shot` for a path that must arc or land.
4. The rendered file: `npx hyperframes audio <video> --json` shows whether sound is there, where it hits and how loud it is. You cannot hear it; say so.

Trust the numbers over your eye where they disagree: a clipped label or a 0.6 s line looks fine on a contact sheet.

## 2. What to look for

First, describe each beat frame in one sentence as a stranger would, naming every object; an object you would have to explain ("those bars are mirrors") is a P0. Then read the beat frames in order: do they tell a story a stranger follows, each one causing the next? Compare each with its shot in `SPEC.md`; what does not match is a note. Then name every default the frames show (`spec.md` "BANNED by default", or one not on the list yet), add each to the BANNED line, and fix them before anything else.

Then go through the sheets once per question:

| Question                      | What it catches                                                                                                                                    |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Does it read as what it is?   | A shape that reads as another object, a material that reads as plastic, a product screen that reads as a mockup, a face or mascot that reads wrong |
| Does the subject separate?    | Subject and ground too close in value, two focal points in one frame, the eye with nowhere to go                                                   |
| Framing and contact           | Crops, text at the edge or under platform UI, collisions at a seam, things floating that should touch                                              |
| Timing as a first-time viewer | A read shorter than its words (`story.md` §6), something that pops on with no move, a jump at a cut, everything moving at once on one curve        |
| Tells                         | Which items of `story.md` §8 and `motion.md` "Defaults that look generated" are on screen                                                          |
| The pictures alone            | With the words covered, do the beat frames still tell the storyline?                                                                               |
| The phone sheet               | Can every line meant to be read be read at 360 px?                                                                                                 |

Write each problem as one line: `t=4.2s · where · problem → exact change · what stays`. Rank them:

- **P0** breaks the read or the contract: unreadable, wrong, broken, a tell in the hero shot.
- **P1** weakens the film: a dead stretch, a soft payoff, a seam that jumps.
- **P2** polish.

Fix every P0 and the P1s worth their time: text first, then timing, then detail. Then snapshot only what you changed, once. A second pass only when a P0 is still open. Never score the film out of 10: a score finds nothing to fix. When a fix does not hold, snapshot the frames on either side of the problem, list every difference, and change only the line that causes it. A film that feels busy: remove a third of the motion and keep the moves that lead the eye.

A fresh pair of eyes, when your host can start a sub-agent: give it only `STORYBOARD.md` and the three sheets, ask for P0 and P1 lines in the format above, and keep editing to yourself. Commit or copy the project before you fix, so a fix that makes things worse can be rolled back.

- the creative calls you made, and the storylines you did not build;
- what you measured and what you only looked at; what nobody checked (the sound was measured, not heard);
- the weakest shot, and what you would change with more time;
- warnings you kept on purpose, and why.

# lint, check, snapshot

Use `lint` for fast static feedback while iterating. Use `check` as the required final gate: it reruns the same linter, then audits runtime, layout, motion, and contrast in one browser session. Do not chain a redundant standalone `lint` immediately before `check`. `snapshot` is the standalone utility for capturing still frames and zoomed crops. `validate`, `inspect`, and `layout` still run but are deprecated: `check` covers all of them in one invocation.

## Discipline (motion-heavy work)

When the composition is animation-driven, run the checks before you reach for `preview` or `render`:

- Run `lint` after the first HTML pass for early feedback. It is an iteration aid, not a separate final gate.
- Run `check --snapshots` at the first full pass: the overview frames and per-finding crops show you what the auditor saw.
- Look at the PNGs before tuning automated warnings: your eye catches what the auditor misses, and the auditor catches what your eye misses.
- Treat layout errors as defects unless a snapshot proves the layering is intentional, in which case mark it with `data-layout-allow-overflow` / `data-layout-allow-overlap` / `data-layout-allow-occlusion` / `data-layout-allow-caption-zone` (caption band only).
- State motion intent in a `*.motion.json` sidecar so `check` verifies it automatically (entrances firing under seek, stagger order, in-frame, liveness). This is the closest automated proxy for "watch the MP4" and catches render-vs-preview bugs the eye misses (see **Motion verification** below).

## lint

```bash
npx hyperframes lint                  # current directory
npx hyperframes lint ./my-project     # specific project
npx hyperframes lint --verbose        # info-level findings
npx hyperframes lint --json           # machine-readable
```

Lints `index.html` and all files in `compositions/`. Reports errors (must fix), warnings (should fix), and info (with `--verbose`). Catches missing `data-composition-id`, overlapping tracks on the same `data-track-index`, unregistered timelines, and GSAP/CSS transform conflicts.

`<video>`/`<audio>` work at any nesting depth, including inside a `compositions/*.html` sub-composition or a wrapper `<div>`: the runtime discovers media with a flat DOM query and seeks/decodes it wherever it lives (`packages/core/src/runtime/{media,startResolver}.ts`). After a render, `snapshot` each scene that has a video and confirm the panel actually shows footage (a blank/black panel where a clip should play is a real bug, not a placeholder).

## check

```bash
npx hyperframes check                    # current directory: the full browser gate
npx hyperframes check ./my-project       # specific project
npx hyperframes check --json             # agent-readable envelope {ok, browserSkipped, lint, runtime, layout, motion, contrast, craft, hdr, snapshots}
npx hyperframes check --snapshots        # also write overview frames (annotated) + per-finding crops
npx hyperframes check --samples 15       # denser timeline sweep (default 9)
npx hyperframes check --at 1.5,4,7.25    # explicit hero-frame timestamps
npx hyperframes check --at-transitions   # also sample every tween start/end boundary
npx hyperframes check --tolerance 4      # allowed overflow px before reporting (default 2)
npx hyperframes check --timeout 30000    # initial render-ready + navigation minimum in ms (defaults: 3000 / 10000)
npx hyperframes check --no-contrast      # skip the WCAG audit while iterating
npx hyperframes check --strict           # exit non-zero on warnings too (default: only errors)
```

One command, one Chrome boot. `check` runs the linter first and skips the browser entirely when lint reports errors. When the browser never ran (lint errors, a linter crash, or a browser launch failure), `browserSkipped` is `true` and the `layout`, `motion` and `contrast` sections are empty, not clean. Otherwise it loads the bundled composition once, wires runtime listeners before navigation, and sweeps one seek grid running every audit per sample:

# Review

You wrote the timeline, so you know what happens; the viewer sees it once, at full speed, often on a phone. Review is how you see the film as they will: as a harsh motion director, not a proud author. `check` catches what is broken; this pass catches what is weak. Run it after `check` passes, on every new film and on any edit that changes timing or layout, before you reply or render.

## 1. Measure, then look

1. `npx hyperframes check --json`. Besides errors it warns on craft it can measure: a line on screen too briefly to read (`line_unread`), more than 3 s with nothing changing (`dead_stretch`), text under 2.6% of the frame's short side (`text_below_floor`), an empty first frame (`first_frame_empty`, the thumbnail on social players), a film over 15 s with no sound (`film_silent`). A warning is a question, not a rule: fix it, or keep it on purpose and say why in the note (a deliberate hold carries `data-hold`).
2. `npx hyperframes snapshot --review` writes three sheets: each scene just after it starts and at its middle, plus each `data-beat`, a strip across every cut (−0.2 s to +0.2 s), and the beat frames at phone width (360 px). Open all three.
3. Motion between the beats: `snapshot --range START,END --frames 8` around the hero move and the payoff; `keyframes --shot` for a path that must arc or land.
4. The rendered file: `npx hyperframes audio <video> --json` shows whether sound is there, where it hits and how loud it is. You cannot hear it; say so.

Trust the numbers over your eye where they disagree: a clipped label or a 0.6 s line looks fine on a contact sheet.

## 2. What to look for

First, describe each beat frame in one sentence as a stranger would, naming every object; an object you would have to explain ("those bars are mirrors") is a P0. Then read the beat frames in order: do they tell a story a stranger follows, each one causing the next? Compare each with its shot in `SPEC.md`; what does not match is a note. Then name every default the frames show (`spec.md` "BANNED by default", or one not on the list yet), add each to the BANNED line, and fix them before anything else.

Then go through the sheets once per question:

| Question                      | What it catches                                                                                                                                    |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Does it read as what it is?   | A shape that reads as another object, a material that reads as plastic, a product screen that reads as a mockup, a face or mascot that reads wrong |
| Does the subject separate?    | Subject and ground too close in value, two focal points in one frame, the eye with nowhere to go                                                   |
| Framing and contact           | Crops, text at the edge or under platform UI, collisions at a seam, things floating that should touch                                              |
| Timing as a first-time viewer | A read shorter than its words (`story.md` §6), something that pops on with no move, a jump at a cut, everything moving at once on one curve        |
| Tells                         | Which items of `story.md` §8 and `motion.md` "Defaults that look generated" are on screen                                                          |
| The pictures alone            | With the words covered, do the beat frames still tell the storyline?                                                                               |
| The phone sheet               | Can every line meant to be read be read at 360 px?                                                                                                 |

## 3. Notes and fixes

Write each problem as one line: `t=4.2s · where · problem → exact change · what stays`. Rank them:

- **P0** breaks the read or the contract: unreadable, wrong, broken, a tell in the hero shot.
- **P1** weakens the film: a dead stretch, a soft payoff, a seam that jumps.
- **P2** polish.

Fix every P0 and the P1s worth their time: text first, then timing, then detail. Then snapshot only what you changed, once. A second pass only when a P0 is still open. Never score the film out of 10: a score finds nothing to fix. When a fix does not hold, snapshot the frames on either side of the problem, list every difference, and change only the line that causes it. A film that feels busy: remove a third of the motion and keep the moves that lead the eye.

A fresh pair of eyes, when your host can start a sub-agent: give it only `STORYBOARD.md` and the three sheets, ask for P0 and P1 lines in the format above, and keep editing to yourself. Commit or copy the project before you fix, so a fix that makes things worse can be rolled back.

## 4. The delivery note

Write `REVIEW.md` at the project root and put its short form in your reply:

- the creative calls you made, and the storylines you did not build;
- what you measured and what you only looked at; what nobody checked (the sound was measured, not heard);
- the weakest shot, and what you would change with more time;
- warnings you kept on purpose, and why.

The next turn reads it before changing anything.

# Sound

Sound is half of how a film feels, and the viewer notices a silent one before any frame. Every judge of frames misses it, so plan it on purpose.

## 1. The default

- **A film over about 15 s that tells something** (launch, explainer, recap, PR video) gets a music bed and sounds on its visible actions, unless the person asked for silence or it is made to play muted (a looping background, a feed that autoplays without sound: then the type and the pictures carry it alone).
- **A voiceover** only when the request or the source calls for one (`SKILL.md`).
- **Each storyline says its sound** in one line (`story.md` §2): the bed's feel and tempo, the one moment the music changes, which actions get effects, or silence and why.
- **Short pieces** (a title card, a sting under 10 s, captions or overlays on footage that has its own sound) follow the request and the footage.

## 2. The clock

- **Narrated**: the voice is the clock. Time each beat's start to its anchor word; text lands on the word that says it.
- **Music only**: the music is the clock. Land the payoff and the mark on its strong beats (`npx hyperframes beats`, then `film.md` "On music"); cuts follow the motion, not the drums.
- Let the sound act out the story when it fits: the old way sits near silence, the music opens when the product appears; the music holds back until the payoff.

## 3. Music

The person's own track first, as given. Else search the catalog (`/media-use`, `bgm`) with the film's feel and tempo, not its subject ("tense minimal pulse building to a bright drop, 120 bpm"), and read a few results before keeping one. Enter at the track's strongest bar, not a quiet intro; end on a bar line with a short fade under the end card.

With no music source (no `heygen` sign-in and no local model), deliver silent and say so in one line with how to add one. Do not spend the run building an audio chain or writing music in code: nobody can hear whether it is good.

## 4. Effects

Few and exact: every effect has a cause on screen, and too many read as a template.

| Sound             | Only on                                        |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| click             | a real cursor click on screen                  |
| whoosh            | a scene cut, or a large card moving fast       |
| soft key tick     | text arriving letter by letter or line by line |
| pop               | a badge, chip or number landing                |
| riser into impact | the payoff or the mark, once in the film       |

- Place a clip so its peak lands one frame after its picture (light arrives before sound; a sound early feels wrong sooner than one late): `npx hyperframes audio <file> --json` reports where it hits, and most files peak after their start.
- Each hit sits 3-6 dB over the bed; a bed with most of its energy under 150 Hz plays as nothing on a phone speaker.
- Rotate two or three takes of a repeated sound; the same whoosh on every cut is the most common tell.
- Over strong music, a typing-heavy film can drop the clicks and keys. No synthesised tones, chimes or dings.

## 5. Levels

Music under a voice sits around 0.14 volume; nothing clips (AI audio often does). Keep each file's true peak at −1 dBTP or lower and the mix around −16 to −14 LUFS for social, `npx hyperframes normalize-audio` to match levels (`/media-use`). Check the rendered file with `npx hyperframes audio <video> --json`: sound present, hits where the picture hits, loudness in range. Say in the delivery note that it was measured, not heard (`review.md` §4).

Serve, render, and share commands.

```bash
npx hyperframes preview                   # foreground on a TTY; persistent in agent shells
npx hyperframes preview --background      # explicit persistent session
npx hyperframes preview --foreground --json # ready JSON, then remain attached
npx hyperframes preview --background --port 4567 # agent-safe custom port (default 3002)
npx hyperframes preview --selection --json # print the current Studio selection and exit
npx hyperframes preview --context --json  # print compact agent context from Studio
```

Hot-reloads on file changes. Opens Studio in the browser automatically — the full timeline editor, where the user can play the video and edit anything by hand before rendering. This is the review surface, not just a viewer.

When handing a project back to the user, use the Studio project URL, not the source `index.html` path:

```text
http://localhost:<port>/#project/<project-name>
```

Use the actual port and project directory name; treat `index.html` as source-code context, not the preview surface. For example, after `npx hyperframes preview --background --port 3017` in `codex-openai-video`, report `http://localhost:3017/#project/codex-openai-video`.

Two ways a handed URL turns out dead — check both before handing it back: the URL is missing its `#project/<project-name>` hash (Studio loads but has no project to open), or the server is not actually running. Bare `preview` automatically creates a managed persistent session in a non-TTY agent shell; `--background` remains the clearest explicit form. Verify the printed URL returns HTTP 200, keep it alive for the whole review, and stop it explicitly with `npx hyperframes preview --stop` afterward. Use the printed URL as-is: HyperFrames URL-encodes project names that contain route metacharacters.

### Agent context from Studio selection

`preview --context` and `preview --selection` are the agent bridge into a running Studio session. They do **not** start a new server; they find the active preview server for the current project, read agent-useful state from Studio, print it, and exit.

Use it when the user gives deictic edit instructions like "change this", "move the selected element", "make the card I clicked bigger", or "fix the current selection":

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection
```

The compact context payload includes the selected element's source file, composition path, current timeline time, `data-hf-id` / selector target, bounding box, text content, and a thumbnail URL for the selected element. Prefer `selection.target.hfId` when present; fall back to `selection.target.selector` only when no stable `data-hf-id` exists. If `selection` is `null`, inspect `errors.selection.code` (for example, `no-selection`).

Keep agent context small by asking only for the slices you need:

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields lint
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection,lint
```

Use `--context-detail full` only when the edit genuinely needs heavy selection fields such as `computedStyles`, `inlineStyles`, `dataAttributes`, or editable text-field metadata:

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection --context-detail full
```

| Code                       | Meaning                                                                    |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `preview-not-running`      | Start Studio first with `npx hyperframes preview --background`.            |
| `ambiguous-preview-server` | Multiple matching Studio servers are open; rerun with one listed `--port`. |
| `preview-port-mismatch`    | The requested `--port` is not one of the matching Studio servers.          |
| `no-selection`             | Studio is open, but the user has not selected an element yet.              |
| `selection-unavailable`    | The running preview server does not expose selection context cleanly.      |

steps.out:
## Motion verification (`*.motion.json` sidecar)

`check` verifies **motion intent** against the same seeked timeline the renderer uses — the closest automated proxy for "render the MP4 and watch it". It catches render-vs-preview bugs layout sampling can't: an entrance reveal the seek lands past, a broken stagger order, an element drifting off-frame mid-tween, a frozen shot.

Drop a `*.motion.json` sidecar next to the composition (matching the html basename when several compositions share a dir). `check` discovers it automatically — no flag, no authoring-framework changes. With no sidecar, `check` behaves exactly as before.

```json
{
  "duration": 6,
  "assertions": [
    { "kind": "appearsBy", "selector": "#headline", "bySec": 0.5 },
    { "kind": "before", "a": "#headline", "b": "#cta" },
    { "kind": "staysInFrame", "selector": ".card" },
    { "kind": "keepsMoving", "withinSelector": ".scene" }
  ]
}
```

| Assertion                      | Fails (code) when                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `appearsBy(selector, bySec)`   | not visible (opacity ≥ 0.5) by `bySec` — `motion_appears_late`                                                              |
| `before(a, b)`                 | `a` does not first appear strictly before `b` — `motion_out_of_order`                                                       |
| `staysInFrame(selector)`       | once visible, its box leaves the canvas — `motion_off_frame`                                                                |
| `keepsMoving(withinSelector?)` | a fully-static window exceeds `maxStaticSec` (default 2s); the film's final 3 s (an end card) never count — `motion_frozen` |

`duration`, `withinSelector`, and `maxStaticSec` are optional. Findings are **errors by default** and appear in the same human and `--json` output as layout findings. A selector that matches nothing is reported as `motion_selector_missing` rather than silently passing — a typo'd selector fails loudly. Use this in the feedback loop instead of eyeballing the render: assert what the motion is supposed to do, and let `check` tell you when the seek diverges from intent.
